title: Week 3: Visualization and ACS Uncertainty
text: This week connected data visualization to statistical uncertainty. We used Anscombe’s Quartet to see why a plot should come before a summary statistic or regression line, then used the grammar of graphics to build plots in ggplot2. We also learned how to retrieve American Community Survey (ACS) data with tidycensus, assess the reliability of ACS estimates, show uncertainty with error bars, and calculate uncertainty for derived measures and changes over time.

title: Week 3: Visualization and ACS Uncertainty
text: This week connected data visualization to statistical uncertainty. We used Anscombe’s Quartet to see why a plot should come before a summary statistic or regression line, then used the grammar of graphics to build plots in ggplot2. We also learned how to retrieve American Community Survey (ACS) data with tidycensus, assess the reliability of ACS estimates, show uncertainty with error bars, and calculate uncertainty for derived measures and changes over time.

title: Week 3: Visualization and ACS Uncertainty
text:
Key Concepts

A dataset can have similar summary statistics but very different visual patterns; plot the data before drawing conclusions.
In ggplot2, aesthetics map data columns to visual properties, while geoms determine how observations are drawn.
ACS data include an estimate and a 90% margin of error (MOE). The MOE is part of the result, not optional background information.
Standard error, coefficient of variation (CV), and relative MOE are related but are not the same measure.
When estimates are summed, converted to proportions, or compared across time, their uncertainty must be calculated as well.

title: Week 3: Visualization and ACS Uncertainty
text:
Note

1. Plot first: Anscombe’s Quartet
Anscombe’s Quartet contains four datasets with nearly identical means, variances, correlations, and regression lines. However, their scatterplots look very different: one is roughly linear, one curves, one is driven by an outlier, and one has almost all points in a vertical line with a single influential point.
The lesson is that numerical summaries are useful, but they are not enough. A regression line or correlation can conceal curvature, outliers, clusters, and unusual data structure. Before interpreting a model, make a plot.


2. The grammar of graphics
A plot maps columns in a dataset to visual properties on a page or canvas. In ggplot2, the basic structure is:
ggplot(data = county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = population)) +
  geom_point()
Here, ggplot() starts the plot, aes() defines the data mappings, and geom_point() draws one point per observation. Layers are added with +.



Data column
Visual property




estimate
x- or y-position


population
x- or y-position


reliability
color


moe
size or an error-bar width



There is an important distinction between mapping a variable and choosing one fixed style:
# Maps the values in reliability to colors and creates a legend
ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = population, color = reliability)) +
  geom_point()

# Makes every point blue; "blue" is not a data column
ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = population)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")
Putting color = “blue” inside aes() tells R that the word “blue” is a data value to map. For a fixed color, place it outside aes().
Common geoms include geom_point() for individual observations, geom_col() for already-calculated values, geom_line() for ordered time series, and geom_errorbar() for uncertainty intervals.


3. Retrieving ACS data
The class example retrieved 2023 ACS 5-year county-level median gross rent. The name on the left of = is a convenient label that we choose; the Census table code identifies the actual ACS variable.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(rent = "B25064_001"),
  state = "NY",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
B25064_001 is the ACS table item for median gross rent. get_acs() returns a tidy table that includes NAME, variable, estimate, and moe. In raw Census API labels and in wide-format output, E denotes an estimate and M denotes a margin of error; for example, B25064_001E is the estimate field.
Different examples in class used different concepts. Median rent was used for the initial retrieval and visualization example, while poverty counts and shares were used to practice derived uncertainty. They should not be treated as the same measure.


4. Reading estimates, MOEs, and reliability
An ACS estimate is a survey-based estimate, not an exact population count. The MOE supplied by the ACS is a 90% margin of error. We can convert it to a standard error with:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]
The value 1.645 is the standard-normal critical value for a two-sided 90% confidence interval. The coefficient of variation is a relative measure of sampling error:
\[
CV = \frac{SE}{estimate} \times 100
\]
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(
    se = moe / 1.645,
    cv = se / estimate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 15 ~ "High reliability",
      cv < 30 ~ "Moderate reliability",
      TRUE ~ "Lower reliability"
    )
  )
For this class rule of thumb, a CV below 15% indicates high reliability, 15–30% indicates moderate reliability, and above 30% indicates lower reliability or higher relative sampling error. A different source may use different cutoffs, so a chart or table should state which standard it follows.
Relative MOE is another useful diagnostic:
\[
Relative\ MOE = \frac{MOE}{estimate} \times 100
\]
It is not the same as CV because CV first converts MOE to standard error. Relative MOE is still useful for finding estimates whose uncertainty is large compared with their magnitude.


5. Showing uncertainty in a chart
The following plot selects counties with the largest relative MOEs for median gross rent. The bar is the estimate; the error bar shows the 90% interval, estimate plus or minus MOE.
county_data %>%
  mutate(
    moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100,
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median gross rent (dollars)",
    title = "New York counties with the largest relative MOEs"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
geom_col(fill = “steelblue”) changes the bar color. If color should instead represent reliability, map the variable inside aes(), for example geom_col(aes(fill = reliability)).


6. Derived uncertainty
Uncertainty has to travel with a calculation. We do not add MOEs directly when we add estimates.








Task
Function
Interpretation




Add several estimates
moe_sum()
MOE for a total made by combining estimates


Make one estimate a share of another
moe_prop()
MOE for a proportion when the numerator is part of the denominator


Divide unrelated estimates
moe_ratio()
MOE for a ratio when neither quantity is a subset of the other



For example, a regional total can be calculated with sum(), while moe_sum() calculates the total’s MOE:
region_summary <- county_data %>%
  summarise(
    total_rent_estimate = sum(estimate),
    total_rent_moe = moe_sum(moe, estimate)
  )
For a poverty share, the numerator is a subset of the total population, so moe_prop() is appropriate. Requesting output = “wide” puts the estimate (E) and MOE (M) columns for each variable on the same row.
poverty_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    below_poverty = "B07012_002",
    total = "B07012_001"
  ),
  state = "NY",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_share = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_share_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  )


7. Comparing two ACS periods
Overlapping confidence intervals are not a sufficient test of whether two ACS estimates differ. Instead, calculate the standard error of the difference, then construct a confidence interval for the change.
For two independent estimates:
\[
SE_{difference} = \sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}
\]
\[
z = \frac{estimate_2 - estimate_1}{SE_{difference}}
\]
At the 90% level, the confidence interval for the change is:
\[
change \pm 1.645 \times SE_{difference}
\]
In the classroom example, median income rose from $45,000 ± $8,000 in 2014–2018 to $62,000 ± $11,000 in 2019–2023. The estimated change was $17,000. Converting both MOEs to standard errors gives an \(SE_{difference}\) of approximately $8,268, so the 90% confidence interval for the change is approximately [$3,399, $30,601]. Because this interval does not include zero, the increase is statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90% confidence level.
comparison <- comparison %>%
  mutate(
    change = estimate_2019_2023 - estimate_2014_2018,
    se_1 = moe_2014_2018 / 1.645,
    se_2 = moe_2019_2023 / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )
The interval for a change should be centered on the difference, not on either original estimate. If the interval includes zero, the available ACS evidence does not show a statistically distinguishable change at that confidence level.


8. Main takeaway
A strong ACS visualization does more than display a value. It makes clear what is being measured, shows uncertainty when it matters, and avoids claims that the data cannot support. Plotting, reliability checks, and derived-MOE calculations are all part of the same analytical workflow.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Key Concepts
Three places a file can live:

My computer — where I edit
GitHub.com — where it’s stored
My live site — what the world sees

The loop: Edit → Save → Render → Commit → Push → wait → refresh

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Note

1. What is a website?
In class, we described a website as two things working together:
a folder of .html files + a computer/server that is always online
For this course portfolio, those two parts are handled by Quarto and GitHub Pages:
Quarto        -> creates the .html files
GitHub Pages  -> hosts the website for free
The basic idea is:
.qmd file that I write
        -> Quarto renders it
        -> .html webpage
        -> GitHub Pages publishes it
This means I usually work on the source file, not the final webpage file.


2. Quarto
Quarto is the tool that turns a .qmd file into a webpage.
The simplified relationship is:
.qmd (you write) -> Quarto (machine) -> .html (webpage)
The action that makes this happen is Render:
.qmd -> Render -> .html


3. What happens during Render?
When I click Render, Quarto reads the file from top to bottom.
It does roughly this:

Reads the .qmd file.
Finds code chunks.
Sends R code to R.
Gets results back from R.
Glues text, code, and results into HTML.

This is why Render is more than saving. Save keeps changes on my computer; Render rebuilds the webpage output.


4. Anatomy of a .qmd file
A .qmd file usually has three parts:
YAML header + Markdown text + R code chunks

YAML header
The YAML header goes at the very top of the file and is surrounded by ---:
---
title: "Week 1 Reflection"
description: "My first weekly note"
date: 2026-08-28
---
It tells Quarto information about the page, such as the title, description, and date.
Important YAML rules:

It must be at the very top of the file.
The opening and closing --- lines matter.
Colons need a space after them.
Dates should use the YYYY-MM-DD format.
Quotation marks should be plain English quotation marks.



Markdown text
Markdown text is the written content of the page:
## Reflection

This week, I learned how to set up RStudio and Quarto.

### Smaller Section

- First point
- Second point
Markdown is where I write headings, paragraphs, lists, links, and notes.


R code chunks
R code chunks are sections where R code can be run. A chunk begins with three backticks followed by {r}, contains R code, and ends with three backticks:

```{r}
summary(cars)
```

If I want to show code but not run it, I can use the eval: false option:

```{r}
#| eval: false
summary(cars)
```




5. Source files and output files
The most important file rule is to edit source files, not output files.
Source files are files I write:
index.qmd
about.qmd
weekly-notes/week-01.qmd
assignments/*.qmd
_quarto.yml
Output files are files the machine makes:
docs/index.html
docs/about.html
docs/weekly-notes/week-01.html
the rest of the docs/ folder
The rule is:
Edit the source files. Do not edit or move the output files.


6. Files and folders
The guiding question from the note is:
Who is this file for?
Files for me to write:
index.qmd
about.qmd
weekly-notes/*.qmd
assignments/*.qmd
Files or folders for tools:
_quarto.yml     settings for the whole website
.Rproj          tells RStudio this folder is a project
.gitignore      tells Git what not to track
.Renviron       stores secrets for R, such as API keys
docs/           website output for the internet
_freeze/        Quarto cache or frozen output


7. Index
On the web, index.html is the default page for a folder. If I ask for a folder URL, the server usually gives me that folder’s index.html.
Example:
website folder URL -> index.html inside that folder
For the portfolio website:
index.qmd -> Quarto render -> docs/index.html
That is why the homepage source file is named index.qmd.


8. Git / GitHub.com / GitHub Desktop
These three are related, but they mean different things:
Git             version tracker
GitHub.com      website that stores a copy of my folder
GitHub Desktop  buttons that tell Git what to do
Git is mostly invisible and runs on my computer. GitHub.com stores the online copy. GitHub Desktop is the app I use to tell Git when to commit and push.


9. Commit and push
Commit and push are two different actions:
Commit = save a labeled snapshot on my computer
Push   = send that snapshot to GitHub.com
Commit happens locally. Push sends the committed version online.


10. R Script
An R script is different from a .qmd file.
R script = code only
.qmd     = writing + code + results
An R script is useful as a sandbox for trying code. A .qmd file is useful when I want to combine explanation, code, and output in a webpage or report.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in New York State. I compare the margins of error for these estimates to identify which counties’ rent data are measured most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state    <- "NY"             # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25064_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 62  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York      B25064_001     1252    22
2 36003 Allegany County, New York    B25064_001      754    33
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       B25064_001     1436    11
4 36007 Broome County, New York      B25064_001      914    26
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York B25064_001      759    30
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York      B25064_001      895    39


I get 62 rows, which match the number of counties in New York State.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York        860    95   11.0 
 2 Schuyler County, New York        858    75    8.74
 3 Greene County, New York          993    79    7.96
 4 Lewis County, New York           821    59    7.19
 5 Orleans County, New York         877    60    6.84
 6 Yates County, New York           802    46    5.74
 7 Wyoming County, New York         782    44    5.63
 8 Cortland County, New York        911    50    5.49
 9 Chenango County, New York        819    44    5.37
10 Livingston County, New York      912    48    5.26


Hamilton County has the largest relative margin of error for median gross rent in New York State. Its estimated median gross rent is $860, with a margin of error of $95, or about 11.0% of the estimate.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    51
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate           10


Among New York’s 62 counties, 51 are classified as high confidence, 10 as moderate, and 1 as low confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York        1252     22  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York       754     33   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York         1436     11 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York         914     26  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York    759     30   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York         895     39   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        381479.
2 Low confidence           1          5102 
3 Moderate                10         41178.


I use the 5% and 10% thresholds established in the previous section so that each reliability category has the same meaning throughout the analysis. This ensures that the population comparison uses the same county classifications as the earlier reliability summary.
High-confidence counties have an average population of about 381,479, while moderate-confidence counties average about 41,178. The only low-confidence county, Hamilton County, has a population of 5,102. This pattern suggests that median gross rent estimates are less reliable in counties with smaller populations, although the low-confidence category contains only one county.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
This analysis shows that New York’s smallest counties tend to have the least reliable median gross rent estimates. Hamilton County is the clearest example: its estimated median gross rent is $860 with a margin of error of $95, or about 11.0 percent. It is the only low-confidence county under the 10 percent cutoff and has only 5,102 residents. Schuyler County has the next-highest relative margin of error at 8.7 percent, followed by Greene County at 8.0 percent.
These differences reflect how the American Community Survey works. The ACS draws estimates from a sample rather than counting every household. Smaller counties generally contain fewer sampled households, so a small number of responses can have a larger effect on their estimates. In these results, high-confidence counties average about 381,479 residents, compared with 41,178 in moderate-confidence counties and 5,102 in the low-confidence county. This pattern indicates that estimates become less precise as county population decreases.
If a state agency allocated housing assistance using median gross rent while treating every estimate as equally certain, small rural counties could be harmed. An underestimated rent could make a county appear less burdened and cause it to receive too little funding, while an overestimate could divert funds from places with greater need. Renters in Hamilton, Schuyler, and Greene Counties may therefore be especially vulnerable. Agencies should consider both the estimates and their margins of error, and they should avoid making major funding decisions based on small differences that may reflect sampling uncertainty.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
We reviewed the portfolio workflow, took a quiz, and began working with two core tools for public-policy data analysis:

dplyr, an R package for transforming tables.
tidycensus, an R package for downloading Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data.

The class connected data manipulation with an important data source: Census geography and ACS estimates.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Concepts

An object stores a value or a table in R.
A function takes an input, does something, and returns an output.
A tibble is a modern kind of data frame: observations are rows and variables are columns.
dplyr verbs make table operations readable: filter rows, select columns, create variables, sort rows, and summarize groups.
The Decennial Census counts the population every ten years; the ACS is a continuous sample survey that provides estimates and uncertainty.
A GEOID is a geographic identifier and should be stored as text so its leading zeros are preserved.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Note

1. Where R code lives
Code typed directly into the Console is useful for trying something out, but it disappears from the record of the project. Save reusable code in an R script, or put code and its results in a Quarto code chunk.
Console      -> temporary experiment
.R script    -> reusable code
.qmd file    -> writing + code + rendered results
For example, this line creates an object named result:
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000)
result                  object that will hold the output
<-                      assignment operator
filter()                function (a dplyr verb)
counties                input data
population > 50000      condition / argument
# comment               explanation for people; R does not run it
<- is the usual R style for assignment. = can also assign an object in many simple cases, but it is also used to name function arguments, so using <- makes the intent clearer.


2. Packages: install once, load each session
A package is a collection of functions. Install it once on a computer, then load it again whenever a new R session needs it.
# Run once on a computer
install.packages("dplyr")
install.packages("tidycensus")

# Run at the start of each new R session
library(dplyr)
library(tidycensus)


3. Tibbles and dplyr verbs
A tibble is a table. Each row is one observation, and each column is one variable.



name
income
moe
moe_pct




Adams
78,975
3,334
9


Berks
74,617
1,191
12


Bucks
104,200
1,502
11



The most common dplyr verbs are:
filter()                    keep rows that meet a condition
select()                    keep or reorder columns
mutate()                    add or change a computed column
arrange()                   reorder rows; use desc() for descending order
group_by() + summarize()    turn many rows into group-level summaries
For example, first keep counties whose margin of error is more than 10%; then sort them from highest to lowest; then keep only the name and percentage:
step_1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)
step_2 <- arrange(step_1, desc(moe_pct))
step_3 <- select(step_2, name, moe_pct)
The resulting table is:



name
moe_pct




Berks
12


Bucks
11



The same work can be written as a pipeline. Both %>% and |> mean roughly “and then.”
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(name, moe_pct)


4. Decennial Census and the ACS
The two Census Bureau products answer different questions:









Product
What it provides
Geography
Important limitation




Decennial Census
A count of the full population every 10 years
Down to Census blocks
Does not provide the full range of social and economic characteristics


American Community Survey (ACS)
Annual estimates for income, education, housing, commuting, poverty, and more
ACS 5-year data reach tracts and block groups
Results are estimates, so they include uncertainty



For ACS data, keep two values in mind:
Estimate (E)          the estimated value
Margin of Error (M)   the uncertainty around that estimate
The ACS uses a sample rather than a complete count. Its 1-year product is the most current, but it is available only for larger areas; the lecture used a 65,000-person threshold. Its 5-year product combines five years of responses, works for nearly all geographies, and is generally the appropriate choice for Census tract or block-group analysis.
ACS 1-year  -> more current; fewer and usually larger geographies
ACS 5-year  -> less current; more precise for small-area analysis
ACS 3-year estimates have been discontinued. A 2016 ACS 5-year estimate, for example, pools responses collected from 2012 through 2016.


5. Census geography and GEOIDs
The basic Census geographic hierarchy is:
state -> county -> Census tract -> block group -> Census block
Census tracts are useful approximations of neighborhoods, but they are not official neighborhood boundaries. They are designed to contain roughly 1,200 to 8,000 people (with an ideal size of about 4,000), and their boundaries can change over time. When comparing historical tract data, resources such as NHGIS and the Longitudinal Tract Database (LTDB) can help.
A GEOID uniquely identifies a geographic unit. For example, the Census tract GEOID 42101000100 contains:



Part
Digits
Meaning




42
2
Pennsylvania


101
3
Philadelphia County


000100
6
Census tract



GEOIDs are identifiers, not quantities. Store them as character strings:
"01001"  # correct: leading zero is preserved
1001     # not appropriate for an identifier: the leading zero is lost


6. ACS variable codes and tidycensus
ACS variables follow a structured naming system. In B19013_001E:



Part
Meaning




B19013
table number


001
line number within the table


E
estimate (M means margin of error)



Use load_variables() to search the available variables for a given year and survey:
library(tidycensus)

variables_2023 <- load_variables(2023, "acs5", cache = TRUE)
get_acs() downloads data. This example retrieves Pennsylvania county-level median household income and total population from the 2023 ACS 5-year release:
library(tidycensus)

data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    total_population = "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


7. Long (tidy) and wide data
The same information can be arranged in two useful ways:








Format
One row represents
Best for




Long / tidy
one geography x one variable
cleaning, filtering, visualization, and repeated operations across variables


Wide
one geographic unit
analysis, modeling, and joining with other datasets



For example, long data have a variable, estimate, and moe column, so Adams County appears once per ACS variable. Wide data keep one Adams County row but use separate columns such as median_incomeE and total_populationE.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Reflection
This week, I learned how R can transform tables with dplyr and how ACS data combine estimates with measures of uncertainty. I also learned that Census geography and GEOIDs matter before analysis begins.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Questions I Still Have

How should I interpret a margin of error when comparing two counties or two Census tracts?
When should I use long data instead of wide data in a real analysis?

title: Assignment3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
I analyze Alfred Lubrano’s 2018 WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer article, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.” The article reports that Eastwick’s poverty rate increased from 12 percent in the 2006–2010 ACS period to 26 percent in the 2013–2017 ACS period. It also states that the newer figures come from the American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates.
The article reports results for Philadelphia neighborhoods, but neighborhoods such as Eastwick are not official Census geographies. The Census Bureau publishes ACS data for Census tracts, which have GEOIDs and defined boundaries. Since the article does not provide its tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk or boundary file, I cannot exactly reproduce its neighborhood-level estimates. Therefore, I reconstruct and test the article’s general poverty-change claim at the Census-tract level for Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania.
Source article: https://whyy.org/articles/new-census-figures-on-philly-neighborhoods-show-inequality-high-numbers-of-whites-living-in-poverty/



I use ACS detailed table B17001, Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age. The table provides a poverty count and its margin of error, as well as the population for whom poverty status is determined.

B17001_001: Total population for whom poverty status is determined. I use this as the denominator.
B17001_002: Population with income in the past 12 months below the poverty level. I use this as the numerator.

For each Census tract, the poverty rate will be calculated as:
\[
\text{Poverty rate} =
\frac{\text{B17001\_002}}{\text{B17001\_001}}
\]
These variables match the article’s general discussion of overall poverty rates. They do not measure poverty only for a specific age group, sex, or race. The article also discusses white poverty in Holmesburg, but that would require a separate race-specific analysis and a clear definition of “white” that the article does not provide. I therefore focus this analysis on overall poverty.


Show code
# Get data
get_poverty <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = c(
      below_poverty = "B17001_002",
      total = "B17001_001"
    ),
    state = "PA",
    county = "Philadelphia",
    year = yr,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr)
  )
}

# Retrieve and combine tract-level poverty data.
poverty_change <- bind_rows(
  get_poverty(2010),
  get_poverty(2017)
)




Show code
poverty_change %>%
  count(period, name = "Number of Census tracts") %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("ACS period", "Number of Census tracts")
  )



Table 1. Census tracts retrieved from ACS 5-year data


ACS period
Number of Census tracts




2006-2010
384


2013-2017
384








I use the 2010 ACS five-year release to represent the article’s 2006–2010 period, and the 2017 ACS five-year release to represent its 2013–2017 period. I specify survey = "acs5" because the article explicitly identifies its data as ACS five-year estimates. The five-year ACS is also the appropriate product for this assignment because it publishes estimates for Census tracts. The ACS one-year product (acs1) does not provide tract-level estimates, so it cannot support this tract-level comparison.
The article does not state its exact Census table, poverty-rate denominator, tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk, or statistical testing method. I therefore make several assumptions. First, I assume its overall poverty-rate figures correspond to the ACS definition in table B17001. Second, I assume that Philadelphia County is the appropriate geography for the City of Philadelphia. Third, I use Census tracts as the analysis unit because the article’s custom neighborhood boundaries are unavailable. Finally, I assume that matching tracts by GEOID permits comparison between the 2010 and 2017 ACS releases; I will check for unmatched GEOIDs before calculating change.
The two ACS periods do not overlap. The first period contains data from 2006 through 2010, while the second contains data from 2013 through 2017. Because they have no years in common, this comparison does not reuse the same annual ACS samples in both estimates. However, these are still pooled five-year survey estimates rather than observations of the same individuals over time. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as changes in estimated tract-level poverty rates, not as evidence that the same residents became poorer.

title: Assignment3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2 — Test

Check missing values
First, I calculate poverty rates and their margins of error for all returned tract-period observations. I do not remove missing values at this stage.


Show code
poverty_rates <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE,
      totalE,
      below_povertyM,
      totalM
    )
  )


I then check which Census tracts have missing poverty-rate results in either ACS period.


Show code
missing_tracts <- poverty_rates %>%
  filter(
    is.na(poverty_rate) |
    is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  ) %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    NAME,
    period,
    totalE,
    totalM,
    below_povertyE,
    below_povertyM,
    poverty_rate,
    poverty_rate_moe
  )

missing_tracts

# ℹ 1 more variable: poverty_rate_moe <dbl>


I do not treat missing values as zero. A poverty rate cannot be calculated when the poverty-status universe is zero or when the ACS does not provide the required estimate or margin of error. I therefore exclude only these tract-period observations from the statistical comparison.


Show code
poverty_rates_clean <- poverty_rates %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(poverty_rate),
    !is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  )




Reliability
I calculate the coefficient of variation using the poverty-rate margin of error. Following Jurjevich et al. (2018), estimates with a CV below 12 percent are classified as reliable; estimates from 12 to 40 percent are somewhat reliable; and estimates above 40 percent are unreliable.


Show code
poverty_rates_clean <- poverty_rates_clean %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (poverty_rate_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )




Show code
poverty_rates_clean %>%
  count(period, reliability)


# A tibble: 6 × 3
  period    reliability           n
  <chr>     <chr>             <int>
1 2006-2010 Reliable             11
2 2006-2010 Somewhat reliable   321
3 2006-2010 Unreliable           45
4 2013-2017 Reliable             22
5 2013-2017 Somewhat reliable   332
6 2013-2017 Unreliable           22


The table below makes the reliability classification visible for the 15 tracts with the largest coefficients of variation in the most recent ACS period. I show the least reliable estimates rather than hiding them because high sampling uncertainty is directly relevant to interpreting apparent change.


Show code
poverty_rates_clean %>%
  filter(period == "2013-2017") %>%
  mutate(
    reliability_symbol = case_when(
      cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    tract = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    rate = poverty_rate,
    rate_moe = poverty_rate_moe
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  select(reliability_symbol, tract, rate, rate_moe, cv, reliability) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Fifteen least reliable tract poverty-rate estimates",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia County, 2013-2017 ACS five-year estimates"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    reliability_symbol = "",
    tract = "Census tract",
    rate = "Poverty rate",
    rate_moe = "MOE",
    cv = "CV (%)",
    reliability = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  fmt_percent(columns = rate, decimals = 1) %>%
  fmt_percent(columns = rate_moe, decimals = 1) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = cv, decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = reliability_symbol) %>%
  tab_source_note(
    "Source: U.S. Census Bureau ACS five-year estimates via tidycensus. Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12% reliable; 12-40% somewhat reliable; > 40% unreliable."
  )

Change over time
Next, I reshape the data so that each tract has one row containing poverty rates and margins of error for both ACS periods.


Show code
poverty_wide <- poverty_rates_clean %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    NAME,
    period,
    poverty_rate,
    poverty_rate_moe
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )


I identify tracts that have usable data in only one period. Those tracts cannot be included in the change test because a difference requires valid estimates and margins of error for both periods.


Show code
incomplete_tracts <- poverty_wide %>%
  filter(
    is.na(`poverty_rate_2006-2010`) |
    is.na(`poverty_rate_2013-2017`) |
    is.na(`poverty_rate_moe_2006-2010`) |
    is.na(`poverty_rate_moe_2013-2017`)
  )

incomplete_tracts


# A tibble: 1 × 6
  GEOID       NAME                 poverty_rate_2006-20…¹ poverty_rate_2013-20…²
  <chr>       <chr>                                 <dbl>                  <dbl>
1 42101980600 Census Tract 9806, …                 0.0978                     NA
# ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​`poverty_rate_2006-2010`, ²​`poverty_rate_2013-2017`
# ℹ 2 more variables: `poverty_rate_moe_2006-2010` <dbl>,
#   `poverty_rate_moe_2013-2017` <dbl>


The ACS reports 90 percent margins of error. I divide each MOE by 1.645 to calculate its standard error, combine the two standard errors to calculate the standard error of the difference, and multiply by 1.645 to obtain the 90 percent margin of error for the change.


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2006-2010`),
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2013-2017`),
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_moe_2006-2010`),
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_moe_2013-2017`)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    change = `poverty_rate_2013-2017` -
      `poverty_rate_2006-2010`,

    se_1 = `poverty_rate_moe_2006-2010` / 1.645,
    se_2 = `poverty_rate_moe_2013-2017` / 1.645,

    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,

    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,

    change_direction = case_when(
      significant & change > 0 ~ "Significant increase",
      significant & change < 0 ~ "Significant decrease",
      TRUE ~ "Not distinguishable from zero"
    )
  )

change_counts <- poverty_tested %>%
  count(change_direction)

change_counts


# A tibble: 3 × 2
  change_direction                  n
  <chr>                         <int>
1 Not distinguishable from zero   313
2 Significant decrease             27
3 Significant increase             36


Of the 376 Census tracts with usable estimates in both periods, 63 show a statistically detectable poverty-rate change at the 90 percent confidence level. The remaining 313 tracts do not show a change that is statistically distinguishable from zero.


Show code
ggplot(change_counts, aes(x = change_direction, y = n, fill = change_direction)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.15) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Significant increase" = "#C85A5A",
      "Significant decrease" = "#4F81BD",
      "Not distinguishable from zero" = "#8A8A8A"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title = "Results of the tract-level poverty-rate change test",
    subtitle = "90% confidence tests for 376 matched Philadelphia census tracts",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of census tracts",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS five-year estimates via tidycensus."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()





Most Philadelphia census tracts did not have a statistically detectable change in poverty rate.






Show code
change_plot_data <- poverty_tested %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(change))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  mutate(
    tract = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    change_pp = change * 100,
    moe_diff_pp = moe_diff * 100,
    direction = case_when(
      change > 0 ~ "Increase",
      TRUE ~ "Decrease"
    )
  )

ggplot(change_plot_data, aes(x = reorder(tract, change_pp), y = change_pp)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = direction), width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = change_pp - moe_diff_pp, ymax = change_pp + moe_diff_pp),
    width = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Increase" = "#C85A5A", "Decrease" = "#4F81BD")) +
  labs(
    title = "Largest statistically detectable poverty-rate changes",
    subtitle = "Twenty largest absolute changes, 2006-2010 versus 2013-2017",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    fill = NULL,

title: Assignment3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate

Supported
The tract-level analysis supports a limited version of the article’s broader claim that poverty changed in parts of Philadelphia. Among the 376 Census tracts with usable estimates for both ACS periods, 36 tracts showed a statistically detectable increase in poverty rate at the 90 percent confidence level. This result is consistent with the article’s general argument that some places in Philadelphia experienced worsening poverty after the earlier 2006–2010 period.
However, this evidence does not support a claim that poverty increased everywhere in Philadelphia. Twenty-seven tracts showed statistically detectable decreases, while 313 tracts had changes that were not distinguishable from zero. The tract-level evidence therefore indicates a mixed pattern of change rather than a uniform citywide increase in poverty.


Not supported
No specific neighborhood-level numeric claim in the article can be classified as directly not supported by this analysis. A tract with a numerical increase that is not statistically distinguishable from zero should not be described as having a confirmed increase. However, because the article reports custom neighborhood estimates while this analysis uses Census tracts, a tract-level non-significant result does not directly contradict a neighborhood-level claim.


Cannot be determined
The article’s specific claim that Eastwick had the largest poverty-rate increase of any Philadelphia neighborhood, rising from 12 percent to 26 percent, cannot be determined from the available analysis. The article does not publish the tracts included in Eastwick or the neighborhood boundary used to calculate its reported rate. As a result, I cannot reproduce the article’s exact numerator, denominator, or margin of error for Eastwick.
The Fairhill claim of a 61 percent poverty rate also cannot be determined for the same reason: Fairhill is a neighborhood rather than a Census geography. Similarly, the Holmesburg claim about white poverty cannot be evaluated with the current analysis because I use overall poverty table B17001, not a race-specific poverty measure. The article also does not define exactly how it measures “white” residents or publish its neighborhood aggregation method.

title: Assignment3: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
New Census estimates show that poverty changed unevenly across Philadelphia between 2006–10 and 2013–17. Of 376 Census tracts with comparable estimates, 36 recorded a statistically detectable increase in poverty, while 27 recorded a detectable decrease. In most tracts, the apparent change could not be separated from normal survey uncertainty. The data therefore show evidence of worsening poverty in some places, but not a uniform increase across the city. They also cannot confirm the article’s exact neighborhood figures, including Eastwick’s reported rise, because those figures rely on neighborhood boundaries that were not published.
